seed_variation.verdict: Only one seed was run, so there is no seed variation to measure.
seed_variation.why: A hosted LLM cannot be seeded: our seeds only reach local random generators, and the provider's sampling (temperature etc.) is fixed for this model. So every run can give different text, and the spread across seeds measures the model's own run-to-run variation. Each seed repeats every API call. Each seed sets Python random, NumPy and torch. PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed to the FIRST seed for the whole run.

predictions.SY0103a: The team designed a voice-controlled kitchen timer with a unique wake word, physical backup button, and multiple simultaneous timers, while debating power options and voice confirmations. As the meeting concluded, tasks were assigned for components, voice commands, market research, and wake word naming, leading up to the next functional design session.
predictions.SY0103b: The team reviewed user research highlighting issues with alarm audibility, greasy buttons, and user confusion over multiple timers, leading them to revise their plan to two numbered timers with escalating volume and audio feedback. Regarding pricing, market research showed resistance to twenty-five euros for a standard timer, but positive reception when pitched as a hands-free gift gadget. The team selected 'Kiko' as the working name, while parking the two-digit display idea and power source decision pending cost breakdowns and input from the absent Tomasz.
predictions.SY0103c: The team reviewed cost breakdowns and competitor pricing, concluding that an offline, app-free device at twenty-five euros is competitive. Priya shared Kiko wake word testing results with minor false triggers, and Tomasz was asked to consult the supplier about tuning. The industrial designer proposed a round, wipeable puck design with the entire top as a soft rubber button and a display in the middle. The meeting concluded with assigning tasks for colour options, a rough physical model, and display behavior details.
predictions.SY0103d: The project manager opened the final detailed design meeting to review Tomasz's physical model, Priya's display and buttons, Ben's colours, and costs. The team evaluated the design against initial goals, confirming hands-free voice operation, a large top button, an eighty-five decibel ramping alarm, and a twenty-five dollar target price enabled by offline functionality. Finally, the team reviewed action items and concluded the meeting.

Priya will contact Marta about speaking with cafe owners at the fair, and the team scheduled the next functional design meeting for shortly.
predictions.SY0110b: The team reviewed cup design details, confirming polypropylene with a ninety millimeter rim, stackable dimensions, and a cafe logo. Finally, the project manager recapped the decisions and action items before closing the meeting.
predictions.SY0110c: The team reviewed dishwasher test results from Cafe Lindner, resolving to use in-mould labelling and a ribbed band. They agreed to launch with a single three hundred millilitre size in slate grey. The user interface designer presented the counter return flow for cracked cups, leading to assigned tasks for quotes, badge design, and a staff guide. Finally, the project manager agreed to handle the management question regarding lost cup costs and meeting minutes.
predictions.SY0110d: The team reviewed the manufacturing quote, agreeing to order ten thousand units at one euro fifty-four each with a six thousand euro mould cost, and discussed covering unreturned cup gaps with partner fees. Marketing Expert wrote a staff guide on cracked cups for lamination, while Industrial Designer specified a three hundred millilitre slate grey polypropylene cup with an embossed return deposit value. Project Manager noted the window badge design is basically final and will ask Jonas for the print file when he recovers. Industrial Designer confirmed an eight-week lead time for the mould and initial batch. Finally, the team confirmed management requirements, and Project Manager agreed to write the final report and minutes.

The team agreed to use the industrial board with the pre-licensed engine for better voice quality, and Priya presented the evaluation criteria. predictions.SY0209a: The team designed the Learnly seven-inch educational tablet case, discussing screen protection alternatives like raised lips and wipeable, easy-to-clean materials. Finally, the project manager reassigned the tablet case market price research to Tomasz, swappable covers were dropped from the scope, and the meeting concluded with action item assignments for the next session.
predictions.SY0209c: The team reviewed survey results, pricing, supplier quotes, and design sketches for the tablet case, agreeing on a twenty-five euro upper price limit. Ben shared an initial quote of eight forty, and Priya presented sketches featuring a top handle and port cut-outs, to which the team added a wedge back for protection and a name tag window. They decided to launch with a strong blue and a lime green, keeping to two colours to manage minimum order quantities, and dropped the idea of a stylus slot. The supplier raised the question of whether the case classifies legally as a toy, which could involve extra safety rules. Total costs sit at nine thirty before the name window, keeping the price comfortable. For the next detailed design meeting, Ben will provide a revised quote, Priya will update the sketches, Tomasz will create final design criteria, and the project manager will handle the minutes, with no further points raised before closing the meeting.
predictions.SY0209d: The project manager opened the final detailed design meeting by reviewing cost estimates and choosing the molded foam pocket, while Priya presented updated sketches with a landscape name tag pocket. Tomasz then reviewed the six evaluation criteria, which the team scored, and the team dismissed a shoulder strap due to safety risks and added cost. Finally, the project manager reviewed the final decisions including the twenty-five euro price, and assigned action items for the report and supplier drawings before closing the meeting.
predictions.SY0304a: The team held a kickoff meeting for a campus parking display project requested by the university estates office, outlining a four-meeting schedule. They agreed displays should show space numbers and colour-coded indicators, targeting staff, students, and visitors with sustainable solar-powered units. After discussing sensing options and excluding an app from the initial scope, the project manager confirmed the next meeting for the same time next week and agreed to circulate minutes and the project brief.
predictions.SY0304b: The project manager opened the functional design meeting to review survey results, sensing options, and layout choices. The team agreed on a large LED display featuring the car park name and color-coded thresholds, and opted to tap into existing mains power from the barrier supply rather than using solar panels. They then decided to use barrier counters with a nightly reset and manual correction, dropping the per-bay sensor quote. Finally, they discussed a central sign by the main gate, which the project manager will check with the estates office.
predictions.SY0304c: The team settled on a sixty-centimetre layout by Tom with a navy strip, car park name, LED numbers with red warnings, and a big P symbol, encased in all-over navy powder-coated aluminium. Flashing signs were abandoned for safety, and four car parks have mains supply while the library requires a new supply, mounting specs, and estates approval. The signs cost three hundred and ninety pounds each, leaving ten pounds spare, and the team briefly discussed barrier resets and deferred QR codes. The meeting concluded with final sign-offs and plans for the next week.
predictions.SY0304d: The team reviewed quotes, mounting strategies, and Tom's sign layout, signing off pending vector files and noting a total cost of one thousand nine hundred and thirty-two pounds. They confirmed a nightly reset for counter drift and agreed that Priya will spot-check car counts in the first fortnight to see if a midday reset is needed. Finally, they evaluated the design against open day surveys, concluding it meets the brief despite budget constraints, and concluded by running through action items and scheduling the library electrician.
